name: Phenylpropanolamine

lead: Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) was a stimulant-like ingredient in cold remedies and over-the-counter diet pills such as Dexatrim and Acutrim. People took it to eat less and lose weight.
It releases norepinephrine from nerve endings, tightening blood vessels in the nose and, at higher doses, acting on the brain to reduce appetite. Some studies showed weight loss with it.

paras: It was sold as a diet aid and decongestant, usually as a pill. It is no longer a mainstream product and is mentioned today as a former diet-pill ingredient.

It raises blood pressure and heart rate, and a 2000 case-control study linked it to hemorrhagic stroke. The FDA advised against its use in November 2000, and the US, Canada and Australia withdrew it in the following years. It is regulated in the US as an amphetamine precursor.

angle.text: Phenylpropanolamine was a stimulant diet-pill ingredient that suppressed appetite so people ate fewer calories and lost weight. It was removed from the market in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.

lead: Phenylpropanolamine (PPA, also called norephedrine) is a sympathomimetic drug related to ephedrine and amphetamine. For decades it was sold over the counter as a nasal decongestant and as an appetite suppressant in diet aids such as Dexatrim and Acutrim. In looks terms, people used it as a short-term aid to eating less and losing body fat, which is the leaner, more defined physique that many appearance communities pursue.[1][2]

It works mainly by releasing norepinephrine, with weaker dopamine release, which narrows blood vessels in the nasal lining and, at higher doses, acts centrally to dampen appetite. Short-term controlled trials of anti-obesity drugs, including PPA, generally reported more weight loss on active drug than on placebo when combined with a calorie-controlled diet.[1][3] Documented effects also include raised heart rate and blood pressure.[1][4]

A 2000 case-control study in the New England Journal of Medicine reported an association between PPA-containing products and hemorrhagic stroke, particularly among women using appetite suppressants.[5] The US FDA advised against its use in November 2000, and Canada, Australia and later the US removed it from the human market. It is now mostly a historical product, mentioned in weight-loss and bodybuilding forum history alongside ephedrine and the ephedra supplements of the 1990s and 2000s.[1][6]
infobox: Acutrim, Dexatrim, Appedrine, Propagest, Westrim (among others)
Withdrawn from human use in US (FDA 2000-2005), Canada, Australia; veterinary use continues in US

paras: PPA's two main uses were decongestion and appetite suppression. In both roles it was usually taken by mouth in tablets, capsules or combination cold products.[1]

PPA was marketed in over-the-counter and prescription diet products, with brands including Acutrim, Dexatrim and Appedrine.[1] Reviews of obesity drug therapy list phenylpropanolamine among the agents studied for weight loss, and note that most appetite-suppressing drugs produced significantly greater weight loss than placebo in short-term randomised trials of up to a year when paired with a calorie-controlled diet or lifestyle programme.[3] A toxicology review of weight-loss agents covers PPA alongside ephedra, caffeine, clenbuterol and others as historically significant products, and notes that the internet keeps banned products accessible.[6]
Grokipedia's summary says its efficacy for weight loss has been questioned relative to its side effects.[2]
Its larger historical use was as a nasal decongestant, usually combined with other cold-remedy ingredients.[1]

subs.h: Use in bodybuilding and fat-loss communities
paras: On T Nation forums in the early 2000s, members discussed norephedrine as one of several stimulant fat-burners, in threads about fat-loss diets and supplement stacks, sometimes alongside ephedrine and other products.[7][8] One thread debated whether combining norephedrine with ephedrine was advisable from a health standpoint.[8] After ephedra and PPA restrictions, a forum member described the sequence in which supplement makers replaced norephedrine and then ephedra sinica in their formulas.[9]

The most-cited human study of PPA is a case-control design that recruited adults aged 18 to 49 from 43 US hospitals after a subarachnoid or intracerebral hemorrhage within 30 days, comparing their use of PPA-containing products with that of controls. The authors set out to test long-standing case-report links between PPA products, including appetite suppressants, and hemorrhagic stroke.[5]

Older controlled trials examined PPA as a decongestant. A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of a combination tablet containing 5 mg phenylephrine, 45 mg PPA and 200 mg guaifenesin in people with rhinitis found that 14 of 20 subjects reported improvement (P <.05).[10] A 1988 controlled trial examined the cardiovascular and psychological effects of PPA together with caffeine.[4] A Cochrane review of oral antihistamine-decongestant-analgesic combinations for the common cold found the evidence for such combinations to be limited.[11]

Other work concerns pharmacology: in vitro work on ephedrine-related stereoisomers at monoamine transporters,[12] and a review of the vascular effects of trace amines and amphetamines.[13] A Cochrane review of interventions to prevent weight gain after smoking cessation also appears in the literature on appetite-affecting drugs.[14] A general review of psychostimulants places PPA among the phenylpropanolamine-derived stimulant classes.[15]

Common effects are increased heart rate and blood pressure.[1][4] Hemorrhagic stroke has been rarely reported, which prompted withdrawals starting in 2000.[1][5] The FDA estimated 200 to 500 strokes per year among younger adult users.[1] Grokipedia reports a relative risk of 16.6 for women who recently started PPA-containing appetite suppressants in the stroke study; this figure comes from an AI-generated summary.[2]

A review of intracerebral haemorrhage lists hypertension and sympathomimetic drug exposure among recognised mechanisms of bleeding into the brain.[16] Toxicology reviews of weight-loss agents describe the stimulant class as carrying cardiovascular and neuropsychiatric risks.[6]

PPA acts largely by releasing norepinephrine, which indirectly activates adrenergic receptors, with weak direct receptor affinity and weaker dopamine release. It is about 100 to 200 times less potent than epinephrine or norepinephrine, has a half-life of about 4 hours, and roughly 90 percent is excreted unchanged in urine.[1][12] Chemically it is a substituted amphetamine and phenethylamine closely related to ephedrine, pseudoephedrine and cathinone.[1]

A 2003 in vitro study of ephedrine-related stereoisomers found selective actions as substrates of the norepinephrine transporter, consistent with PPA's role as a norepinephrine releaser.[12] According to Wikipedia, oral onset is 15 to 30 minutes, duration about 3 hours, protein binding about 20 percent, metabolism minimal, and elimination depends on urinary pH.[1]

Wikipedia describes the mechanism as indirect: PPA triggers norepinephrine release, and releases dopamine about ten times less potently, and earlier ideas that it directly activated adrenergic receptors were later disproven.[1] Immediate-release forms peak at around 1.5 hours and about 90 percent is excreted unchanged in urine; acidic urine speeds elimination and alkaline urine slows it, and because it is barely metabolized, accumulation is a concern in renal impairment.[1]

Interaction data are limited. Wikipedia cites one study in which PPA roughly quadrupled caffeine levels and another in which it halved theophylline clearance; a 1988 controlled trial examined the cardiovascular and psychological effects of PPA together with caffeine.[1][4]
PPA was first synthesised around 1910 and patented as a mydriatic in 1913. Its blood-pressure effects were studied in the 1920s and 1930s and it was in medical use by the 1930s.[1]

It later became a staple of over-the-counter cold remedies (for example Allerest, Demazin and Dimetapp combinations) and of diet aids sold under names such as Dexatrim and Acutrim.[1] After the 2000 stroke study, the FDA issued a public health advisory in November 2000 recommending against its use, and OTC sale ended by 2005 when it lost its generally-recognised-as-safe-and-effective status.[1][5]

Wikipedia gives the 2000-2001 sequence outside the US: Canada withdrew PPA in May 2001 and Australia followed by July 2001.[1] India banned it in early 2011, but the Madras High Court overturned the ban for pediatric drugs in September 2011.[1]

Under the US Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act of 2005, PPA is controlled because it can be used to make amphetamine. The 2020 CARES Act requires FDA approval before it can return to the market. It remains available by prescription in Sweden and Germany. In June 2024 the FDA approved generic PPA chewable tablets for canine urinary incontinence; veterinary use continues in the US.[1] India banned human use in early 2011, but the ban was overturned in September 2011.[1]

Wikipedia notes that PPA is not on the WADA prohibited list as of 2024 and that clinical studies suggest it is not effective as a performance enhancer; a T Nation discussion of an athlete's doping history nonetheless mentions positive tests for PPA among banned cold-remedy stimulants in the 1980s.[1][17]

Wikipedia says PPA is not approved for human use in the UK and remains available in some places such as Sweden and Germany.[1] Its stereoisomer norephedrine was proposed for UN drug-control schedules in 2000, and in the US PPA is controlled because it can be used to make amphetamine.[1]

In the US, PPA continues to be used in dogs for urinary incontinence caused by a weak urethral sphincter. The brand Proin was first approved in 2011, and in June 2024 the FDA approved generic PPA chewable tablets for this purpose.[1]

PPA is chemically a substituted amphetamine closely related to ephedrine, pseudoephedrine and cathinone.[1] Forum discussions from the early 2000s mention norephedrine alongside ephedrine-based fat burners, and a 2012 toxicology review treats PPA with ephedra, caffeine and clenbuterol among historically significant weight-loss products.[6][7][8]

lore.intro: PPA appears in older bodybuilding and fat-loss forum threads from the early 2000s, mostly as norephedrine in stimulant stacks, and in discussions of products that were reformulated after regulatory action.[7][8][9]
